newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open narrowly mixed before data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open narrowly mixed before data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened narrowly mixed on Friday ahead of two government reports on the economy in March -- one on wholesale prices and the other on retail sales.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 3/32 to 94-3/32 in early trade, yielding 7.10 percent. Two-year notes were unchanged at 98-05, yielding 6.59 percent. Three- and six-month bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.15 percent and 5.39 percent, respectively.

The Labor Department will issue the March Producer Price Index (PPI), expected to be unchanged after a 0.4 percent drop in February. The PPI without its more volatile food and energy components is expected to be up 0.1 percent, according to the average forecast gathered in a Reuters poll.

The Commerce Department will issue retail sales data for March. Sales are expected to be up 0.6 percent after a 0.8 percent February rise, according to Reuters' poll. Excluding autos, sales are expected to be up 0.4 percent after a 0.5 percent ex-autos gain in February.

Analysts said the market will examine the data and economic reports due next week for clues as to whether the Federal Reserve will move at its next policy meeting on May 20. If the market decides conclusively that the Fed will raise rates again in May, U.S. securities prices will have to come down, especially at the front end of the curve, analysts said.

Data that are slightly more benign for the market than expected would prompt short-covering, they said. But they said the potential for friendly data to push the market up would be limited. The bond market will need strong hints that the economy has started to slow before it can rally, they said.

"We would expect the market to focus in on any negatives the reports provide and even friendly numbers are likely to bring only temporary relief," said MMS International economist David Shabelman. "A rally on friendly data would mainly be confined to short-covering and would not bring the change in sentiment needed to .... sustain a rally."
Shabelman said the market's focus would shift to next week's release of the March Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the "threat it brings."
Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, agreed that some people view the risks assigned to the release of economic data as assymetrical.

But some analysts said a case could be made that the market has been establishing a bottom and that it was ready to break out of the range it has been trading in between 7.05 percent and 7.15 percent on the 30-year bond yield.
Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-21/32, yielding 6.44 percent. Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-14/32, yielding 6.76 percent. Ten-year notes were up 3/32 to 95-14/32, yielding 6.89 percent.
